questions.question: For a set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, which set is the convex hull $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$, described from outside?
options: The intersection of all closed sets $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with $V\subseteq S$.
The union of all convex sets $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with $S\subseteq V$.
The intersection of all convex sets $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with $V\subseteq S$.
The set of all linear combinations of finitely many points of $V$.

questions.question: For an arbitrary set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, which argument shows that $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$, the intersection of all convex sets containing $V$, is itself convex?
options: Any intersection of convex sets is convex, and the family is nonempty because $\mathbb{R}^n$ belongs to it.
Every set in the family contains each segment between two points of $V$, so the intersection contains these segments.
Every convex set containing $V$ is closed, and an intersection of closed sets is again a convex set.
The set $V$ lies inside $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$, and convexity passes from $V$ to every set that contains it.

questions.question: For a set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, which condition on $V$ is equivalent to $\operatorname{Conv}(V)=V$?
options: $V$ contains the midpoint of any two of its points.

questions.question: For sets $V,W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, which implication about their convex hulls always holds?
For a nonempty set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, which description of $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$ from inside is correct?
Let $V=\{(0,0),(6,0),(0,3)\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$. Which of the following points lies in the convex hull $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
Let $V=\{(0,0),(4,0),(0,4),(1,1)\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(3,2)$. Which closed halfspace proves that $\boldsymbol{p}\notin\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+x_2^2=1,\ x_2\geq0\}$ be the upper half of the unit circle. Which set is $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
Let $V=\{3,-1,7,2\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Which set is the convex hull $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
Let $V=\{(t,0)\colon t\in\mathbb{R}\}\cup\{(t,1)\colon t\in\mathbb{R}\}$, the union of two parallel lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which set is $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$. Which condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{Conv}(V\setminus\{\boldsymbol{p}\})=\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
options: $\boldsymbol{p}$ lies on the segment between two other points of $V$.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ is a convex combination of finitely many points of $V$.
$\boldsymbol{p}$ does not lie in the interior of $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$.

questions.question: Which property of a set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ always passes to its convex hull, so that $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$ has it whenever $V$ has it?
options: Being contained in a given closed ball.
Being a finite set of points.
Being contained in a union of two disjoint closed balls.

questions.question: For finite nonempty sets $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ in general, which statement about writing a point of $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$ as a convex combination of points of $V$ is correct?
options: The weights are determined uniquely once the points used are fixed.
A point may have several representations, using different points or weights.
A point $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ is represented only as $1\cdot\boldsymbol{x}$.
Each representation gives positive weight to every point of $V$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{(t,t^2)\colon t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ be the parabola in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which set is $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
The set $V=\{\tfrac{1}{k}\colon k\in\mathbb{N},\ k\geq1\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ of reciprocals of the positive integers is infinite. What is its convex hull $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?

Let $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1^2+x_2^2<1\}$ and $V_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon (x_1-2)^2+x_2^2<1\}$ be open unit discs. Which point lies in $\operatorname{Conv}(V_1\cup V_2)$?
With $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$ defined as the intersection of all convex sets $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ with $V\subseteq S$, what is $\operatorname{Conv}(\varnothing)$, and why?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, because a convex combination of no points is the empty sum $\boldsymbol{0}$.
$\varnothing$, because $\varnothing$ is convex and is one of the convex sets containing $\varnothing$.
$\mathbb{R}^n$, because no convex set qualifies and an empty intersection is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
It is undefined, because a convex combination needs at least one point of $V$.

questions.question: Which statement about convex hulls holds for all sets $V,W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$?
Let $V=\{(0,1)\}\cup\{(t,0)\colon t\geq0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$, a closed set consisting of a point and a closed ray. Which set is $\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
Let $V=\{(0,0),(6,0),(0,6),(2,2),(3,3),(1,3)\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$. Which subset $W\subseteq V$ has the fewest points among all subsets with $\operatorname{Conv}(W)=\operatorname{Conv}(V)$?
